opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
When Jesus says, “I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate,” He is revealing something astonishing. He is preparing the disciples for His physical departure, yet at the same time promising that they will not be abandoned. The word “another” is important because it implies that Jesus Himself had already been their advocate, their guide, protector, teacher, and comforter. Now He says the Father will send another in His place.

This Advocate is the Holy Spirit. Not merely a force or inspiration, but the living presence of God dwelling with and within believers. Jesus had walked beside the disciples outwardly, but the Spirit would dwell within them inwardly. Christ’s earthly ministry among them was becoming something even deeper and more universal.

The word translated as “Advocate” carries several meanings at once: comforter, helper, counselor, defender, and intercessor. It is someone who stands beside another. In the Catholic understanding, this is the continuing presence of God guiding the Church after Christ’s ascension.

And this connects directly to the fear and confusion the disciples were experiencing. Jesus had just spoken about hatred from the world, persecution, suffering, and His departure. Naturally, the disciples would wonder how they could endure such things without Him physically present. The promise of the Advocate is Christ’s answer to that fear.

He is essentially saying: You will not carry this mission alone.

The disciples who once hid in fear after the crucifixion later stood publicly before rulers, imprisonment, torture, and death proclaiming Christ without retreat. The transformation between those two realities is one of the great testimonies to the coming of the Holy Spirit in the Acts of the Apostles.

And there is something deeply personal in this promise. Jesus does not merely leave behind teachings, principles, or memories. He leaves His own presence through the Spirit. The Christian life is therefore not simply imitation of Christ from a distance, but participation in His life from within.

So when Jesus says, “I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate,” He is not speaking about replacement. He is speaking about continuation. The visible presence of Christ among them would become the invisible presence of God within them. There is also a profound irony in these passages. The world believes itself enlightened, sophisticated, and wise, yet according to Jesus, it is spiritually blind. Meanwhile, the disciples — ordinary fishermen, tax collectors, and common men — begin perceiving realities hidden from rulers and scholars because they are willing to receive truth rather than control it.

And this still remains true. Two people can witness the same event, hear the same Gospel, read the same words of Christ, and one encounters life while the other sees only religion, mythology, or foolishness. The difference, according to Jesus, is not merely intelligence. It is whether the heart is open to God.
